index.heading: Challenges
index.intro: You are given a state, an operation or a truth table. You build the circuit that produces it. The server runs your circuit with the same engine this page uses and decides — so what is on your screen and what is on the leaderboard can never disagree.
index.order: The order is a curriculum: one qubit before two, a state before an operation, an operation before a truth table. Each challenge assumes the ones above it.

targetNote.state: The target is a state. Your circuit is compared with it up to an overall phase, because two states differing by one are physically the same.
targetNote.unitary: The target is an operation, not a state. What is compared is what your circuit does to every input — so a circuit that happens to get |0…0⟩ right is not enough.
targetNote.truth_table: The target is a truth table. Only the listed basis inputs are checked: it asks what your circuit does to definite bits and nothing about the phases between them.

feedback.solved: Your circuit reaches the target, with a fidelity of {{value}}.
feedback.orthogonal: Your state has no overlap at all with the target. This is not a small correction away — try a different construction rather than a different angle.
feedback.relative-phase: Every magnitude is right and the phases between them are not. The histogram cannot show this; the phasors on each bar can, and so can the amplitude table.
feedback.qubit-order-reversed: Reversing the order of your qubits would solve it. Qubit 0 is the least significant bit here, as it is in Qiskit.
feedback.entanglement-missing: The target is entangled and your qubits are independent. Watch the Bloch arrows: on an entangled qubit the arrow shrinks towards the centre.
feedback.entanglement-unwanted: Your qubits are entangled and the target’s are not. Something is correlating wires that should be left alone.
feedback.too-few-outcomes: Your state reaches {{value}} basis states and the target reaches more. Something is not being put into superposition.
feedback.too-many-outcomes: Your state reaches {{value}} basis states and the target reaches fewer. Something is spreading amplitude where the target has none.
feedback.nearly-there: Close — a fidelity of {{value}}. Look for one wrong angle rather than one wrong gate.
feedback.wrong-qubit-count: Your circuit is on {{value}} qubits, which is not this challenge’s register, so there is nothing to compare it with.
feedback.empty-circuit: There are no gates on the canvas yet.
feedback.gate-not-allowed: This challenge does not allow this gate:
feedback.not-scored: Your circuit was not compared with the target at all, because it uses a gate this challenge does not allow. The fidelity above is not a reading. Take the gate out and submit again.
feedback.no-final-state: This circuit has no single final state, so there is nothing to compare: something in it measures, resets, or depends on a classical bit. Remove it and the whole circuit becomes one operation again.
feedback.gate-budget-exceeded: Your circuit uses {{value}} gates, which is over the budget. The physics above still applies — this is about length, not correctness.
feedback.basis-states-only: Checked on {{value}} basis inputs. A truth table says nothing about superposed inputs: two very different operations can share one.
feedback.rows-wrong: {{value}} of the checked inputs came out somewhere else.
feedback.row-not-a-basis-state: {{value}} of them did not come out as a definite bit pattern at all — the circuit left them in a superposition.
feedback.global-phase-ignored: Your state carries an overall phase of {{value}} radians relative to the target. That is not a difference: no measurement can detect an overall phase, and it was ignored.

superposition.title: A coin in the air
superposition.prompt: Put the single qubit into an equal superposition, so that measuring it gives `|0⟩` half the time and `|1⟩` the other half. One gate is enough.

minus-state.title: The same halves, the other sign
minus-state.prompt: Produce `(|0⟩ − |1⟩)/√2`. Its probabilities are exactly those of the previous challenge — the histogram will look identical — and its phase is not. Watch the phasor on the second bar.

bell-pair.title: Two qubits, one answer
bell-pair.prompt: Produce `(|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2`: two qubits that each look random on their own and always agree with each other. When you have it, both Bloch arrows collapse to the centre of their spheres.

ghz-three.title: All three at once
ghz-three.prompt: Extend the pair to three qubits: `(|000⟩ + |111⟩)/√2`. Three wires, all or nothing.

y-eigenstate.title: A quarter turn
y-eigenstate.prompt: Produce `(|0⟩ + i|1⟩)/√2`. The same two halves again, with the phase a quarter of the way round the circle instead of half.

hadamard-conjugation.title: Z without a Z
hadamard-conjugation.prompt: Build the `Z` gate using only `H` and `X`. The target here is an operation rather than a state: what is compared is what your circuit does to every input, so getting `|0⟩` right proves nothing.

cnot-reversed.title: Turn the arrow around
cnot-reversed.prompt: Build a `CNOT` whose control is qubit 1 and whose target is qubit 0, using only a `CZ` and `H` gates. A `CZ` has no arrow — it treats both wires alike — so the `H` gates are the entire content of the answer: they are what decides which way the `CNOT` points.

swap-from-cnots.title: Exchange, with nothing to exchange with
swap-from-cnots.prompt: Swap two qubits using `CNOT` gates alone. Hardware often has no `SWAP`, and this is what it does instead — which is why moving a qubit across a chip is expensive.

toffoli-truth-table.title: A classical gate, built from quantum ones
toffoli-truth-table.prompt: Flip qubit 2 exactly when qubits 0 and 1 are both `1`, using only `H`, `T`, `T†` and `CNOT`. This one is scored on the eight basis inputs: it asks what your circuit does to definite bits, and nothing about the phases.
